#4000. Monopoly Go x The Simpsons crossover is almost here

After a long wait and exhaustive leaks, the highly-anticipated Simpsons event will finally arrive in Monopoly Go very soon, alongside new content.

Monopoly Go players have been looking forward to a major crossover event for what felt like months, and though most of the details ended up leaking, nothing actually beats official information.

The world of The Simpsons has officially arrived in Monopoly Go, and there's a whole lot for players to dive into. The show's creative team even produced a new animated short, featuring Mr. Monopoly, and Mr. Burns.

Available June 3 through July 29, the new event allows Monopoly Go players to jump in the world of The Simpsons. You'll be able to build, and explore all around multiple iconic locations from the show.

Along the way, you'll run into Simpsons characters like Homer, Marge, Bart, Lisa, and of course, Mr. Burns. Developer Scopely teamed up with the show's creative team to create many references, and Easter Eggs for you to discover. You'll find some of those on chance cards, but most of the world has been changed to be part of The Simpsons, including getting to bribe Chief Wiggum to escape jail.

The developer promises a deeply connected world with Simpsons narratives and characters that alter seasonal maps, and offer unique sticker sets and animated sequences to dive in. Incidentally, this is The Simpsons' first appearance in a mobile-exclusive game in 13 years.

Here's a breakdown of everything you can expect, straight from Scopely:

Episodes: Narrative-driven encounters that create stories inspired by The Simpsons. Episodes play out across seasonal boards, sticker sets, and minigames, all capped off with an animated short.

Sticker sets: Every Episode comes with its own limited-time sticker set, taking cues from the latest Simpsons story. Collectible artwork, character journeys and other rewards are yours to claim for the duration of each Episode.

The Simpsons Run: Every two weeks, a new Springfield character will take over the Free Parking tile, kicking off character-driven runs.

Simpsons-themed Shutdowns and Heists: Monopoly Go's shutdowns and heists get a Simpsons makeover, with Springfield-inspired chaos and disasters.

Bribe Wiggum: This changes Go to Jail to allow players to bribe Chief Wiggum, giving you a chance to earn a bigger reward, but not without introducing an element of unpredictability.

Simpsons chance cards: The chance card collection grows with over 50 Simpsons-themed cards full of memes, references and one-liners from the show.

If you're excited to jump in tomorrow, be sure to check out these Free Monopoly Go Dice Links before you dive into the new content.

#3998. Sea Of Thieves Is Getting A Massively Reduced File Size On Xbox And Other Platforms

Anyone who's planning to play GTA 6 this week seems to be feeling the pinch in terms of storage space, so you might be glad to hear that Sea Of Thieves is getting a ridiculously large reduction in install size this Thursday.

On Xbox Series X, for example, the game is going from over 100GB down to 56.4GB, while players on Xbox One and Xbox Series S are only looking at a mere 25+GB to keep the game installed. An amazing improvement all round!

Here's the full breakdown, including for other platforms like PC and PlayStation:

This will roll out as part of a new update on November 19th, alongside some bug fixes and other minor improvements that are detailed in a video over on the Sea of Thieves YouTube channel (that you can watch up above).

#3997. Ahead of The Witcher 3: Songs of the Past, here's a "lore friendly unofficial expansion to Geralt's life in Toussaint" from a well-established quest modder

While its remastered upgrade might have broken cover in late September, The Witcher 3's extra expansion isn't set to join it until next year. With 2027 still a month and a bit away, a modder's taken it upon themselves to add a few more adventures to Geralt's time in Toussaint, Blood and Wine's gorgeous French-ish duchy, before the bloke from the river heads off to Letten for Songs of the Past.

So far, only the opening chapter of the mod - Annals of the Duchy - has been released. It adds in a new quest about Geralt, with help from either Yen or Triss if either have made the trip out to Toussaint as part of your playthrough, getting into a scrape thanks to a halfling who seems to promise Gerry the chance to juice up his vineyard's vines.

The mod's creator, Jontej, has previously put together a couple of other custom Witcher 3 quests. While they do look to have used AI voices in English versions of those mods, for Annals of the Duchy they've enlisted a cast of human actors for both Enlish and Polish versions.

Jontej has plans to expand this new questline going forwards, having cited specific "plans for an extra storyline involving Syanna", whom you might remember from Blood and Wine's main quest. Given that - spoilers ahead - the mod relies on you having gotten the Blood and Wine ending which sees both Anna Henrietta and Syanna survive, as well as having paid to renovate the gardens of Geralt's vineyard. They add that, when it comes to their additions, the "timeline fits quite well [with] the upcoming official Songs of the Past Expansion, which has been confirmed to take place after the events of the main game/Blood and Wine".

As much as I've argued that, as of right now, I struggle to see how Songs of the Past will manage to outdo Blood and Wine as a satisfying end to Geralt's tale in the Witcher game trilogy, I am intrigued by the idea of a few more modded adventures showing Gerry adjusting to the semi-retired life. After all, Toussaint's got to have a few more dungeons tucked away that're worth temporarily dusting off the White Wolf's twin swords for.

To kick off Annals of the Duchy, you'll need to trigger its first quest by taking a stroll from the Corvo Bianco manor house down to its gardens between 11am and 1pm. It's worth noting that any other mod which messes with Yen, Triss or companions in general has a chance to muck things up as far as Jontej's creation goes.

#3995. Rockstar were "definitely" thinking about giving a Japanese studio the keys to GTA, says former tech director - "I have a name, but I'm not gonna say it"

Obbe Vermeij on ancient plans for a GTA Tokyo

Since time immemorial, North American and European publishers have racked their brains over ways to make their games sell in Japan, ancient heartland of mythical beings like Mario, Sonic, and Polaroid Pete. In the late noughties, Microsoft launched a big push to give Japanese youth the Xbox virus with such targeted console exclusives as Blue Dragon and Lost Odyssey. And Rockstar once dreamed of making a Grand Theft Auto game set in Tokyo.

Speaking to me last week, Rockstar North's former technical director Obbe Vermeij shared a little about the abandoned project. Emphasis on the "little" – it doesn't appear to have gotten very far, despite recently unearthed allusions to "Tokyo PS2" in GTA 5's source code.

Rockstar's parent company Take-Two Interactive filed a trademark for GTA Tokyo back in 2003, the year before the release of the Los Angeles-flavoured GTA: San Andreas. At the time, Rockstar were apparently looking at collaborating with a Japanese studio on the project. "So this was kind above my pay grade," Vermeij told me. "But yeah, there were negotiations with studios, and I have a name, but I'm not gonna say it, because then it becomes like a bigger thing than it is, and I'll probably get it wrong, and I don't know how far the negotiations were, how serious it was. I mean, it was definitely serious. It was the plan. But I don't know how close it got to actually happening."

The game itself would likely have been a contemporary story, not a historical yarn like Rockstar's subsequent Red Dead Redemption. "It definitely had samurai swords in it, I remember that, but I think it was present-day probably," Vermeij went on. "Or sort of not too [far off] - it wasn't, like, sort of the medieval era in Japanese history, or anything. It was definitely not like that."

Vermeij was at Rockstar from 1995 to 2009, where he worked on the first four mainline 3D GTA games, plus some handheld spin-offs. During that time, he says, Rockstar frequently considered the idea of a Grand Theft Auto set outside the United States. "In the same way that we were always thinking about other games, we also thought about cities that would be cool, and it was always the same list," he said. "It was Moscow, London. Istanbul, Rio de Janeiro, maybe Paris and Tokyo. It was always the same ones that people suggested."

Grand Theft Auto has never quite the money-spinner in Japan that it is in North America and Europe. Localised editions of the original three 3D GTA games were published by Capcom, sometime after the original releases, selling a few hundred thousand copies apiece in their launch years.

"I think perhaps [Rockstar's co-founders] the Housers were a little annoyed that GTA wasn't as big in Japan as they thought it deserved to be," Vermeij reflected. "So it kind of made sense to get a local studio to do it. Japanese people actually kind of like different games from westerners a fair bit. For instance, they don't like first person shooters and stuff. So, it made sense to have a Japanese studio have a shot at it, and I think it would have been really cool, because you know, a GTA made by somebody else in Japanese culture – that's something I would probably play."

Take-Two ultimately abandoned their original "GTA Tokyo" trademark in 2008. It's not clear how much Rockstar have considered setting GTA overseas since Vermeij's day, but co-founder Dan Houser (who left the company in 2020) recently told podcaster Lex Fridman that they ultimately decided it wasn't a credible objective.

“We made a little thing in London 26 years ago - GTA London - for the top-down for PS1," he said. "That was pretty cute and fun, as the first mission pack ever for PlayStation 1. I think for a full GTA game, we always decided there was so much Americana inherent in the IP, it would be really hard to make it work in London or anywhere else. You know, you needed guns, you needed these larger-than-life characters. It just felt like the game was so much about America, possibly from an outsider's perspective. But that was so much about what the thing was that it wouldn't really have worked in the same way elsewhere.”

If this article has left you pining for the Shibuya Scramble NPC-tipping sim that will never be, I bring good news: Japanese developers are quite capable of making their own urban open worlders. The obvious go-tos are Sega's Yakuza/Like A Dragon games, with their abundance of lovingly modelled eateries and discount stores. There's also Ghostwire: Tokyo, a respectable first-person parkour sim, though this particular incarnation of Tokyo has a lot of paranormal congestion. All these games have the advantage of being playable on PC right now. As for GTA 6? Who can say, but Vermeij thinks Rockstar might want to port it sooner to get ahead of the slopcomp craze.

#3994. "There is no excuse for what I did," Nvidia CEO says, as affair with an alleged Chinese spy makes the US-China AI race look even more ridiculous

Just saying, Jensen, this probably doesn't happen if you stick to gaming GPUs

Ostensible graphics card company and definite AI giants Nvidia have commissioned an independent investigation into themselves, amid reports that CEO Jensen Huang had an extramarital affair with a suspected Chinese spy.

Per both the New York Times and Nvidia themselves, Nvidia offered to go under the microscope after US intelligence organisations elected to investigate Huang’s paramour, Chinese national Alice Huang (no, uh, relation, and also known as Huang Le), on suspicion of sharing sensitive information with Beijing. The Nvidia-running, leather-jacketed Huang has thus far only copped to an unspecified affair, admitting in an extraordinary public statement that he was "unfaithful to my wife." Still, the two investigations are likely to start a bizarre new leg in the alread-messy AI arms race that the US and China have been indulging in for years.

See, the basis for Huang and Huang’s relationship appears to be the same thing that’s been fucking us as PC owners: data centres and AI hardware. Alice Huang is a former managing director of Megaspeed, a Singapore-based data centre company who’ve bought billions of US dollars’ worth of Nvidia chips – and have been investigated for allegedly getting some of them into the hands of Chinese companies, in defiance of US trade restrictions on goods that might threaten the States’ AI dominance. Possibly also, given both countries’ increasing interest in the technology’s military uses, their perception of national security.

Many of these embargo-dodging accusations originate from after Alice Huang left Megaspeed, though she is now under that separate investigation for intelligence-sharing, and the prospect of any high-tech pillow talk from the lips of someone like Jensen Huang would be very disturbing to the feds indeed. Both Nvidia and their "deeply sorry" CEO deny that he shared sensitive information beyond that required for routine customer/client discussions.

"While the Board has no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised, the Board's inquiry will examine all available information," the company’s statement reads. "Jensen fully supports the review and has committed to cooperating with it. The Board has confidence in Jensen and his leadership team and will provide further updates as appropriate."

In the US-Sino battle of artificial intelligence, Jensen Huang has – as with his marriage – played both sides. He’s undoubtedly been a, perhaps the driving force behind reinventing Nvidia from beloved makers of gaming gear to the US’ number-one purveyors of environment-ruining, brain-polluting slop technology. But after the Biden administration banned American-made GPU exports to China over fears they’d be used to boost the latter’s military capabilities, Huang successfully lobbied Donald Trump into relaxing those restrictions, allowing Nvidia to flog their wares – including their crème de la crème AI GPU, the H200 – to cash-rich Chinese companies.

In a further twist, many of those chips have got mysteriously stuck in Hong Kong import facilities, suggesting the Chinese government in fact wants AI companies to stick to Chinese-made parts. But then, the Hangzhou-based DeepSeek reportedly trained their latest AI model on illicitly-gained Nvidia tech, so there’s either a healthy black market in operation, or the CCP is willing to tolerate the occasional bit of decadent Western silicone if it helps them catch up to the burger-chomping likes of ChatGPT and Claude. Maybe both, and either way, one can see how a well-placed honeypot could prove useful. Allegedly.

Without wanting to pick sides, in a race where I hope both teams lose, it’s also China who have more work to do. The People’s Republic produces a greater proportion of successful 'open' AI models, where the inner workings and even source code is made public, and mines more of the crucial minerals needed to build components and infrastructure. However, US-produced 'closed' models dominate global AI usage, and despite the lack of minerals, its existing data centres are estimated to wield 40 times the combined compute power of China’s. Probably because they just get all the RAM they need from Best Buy instead of digging it up themselves.

#3993. Hardware Review: Nacon Revolution 5 Unlimited - Solid Xbox-Style PS5 Controller Undercuts Its Competition

For the last month, I’ve been levelling up my game with the Nacon Revolution 5 Unlimited, a hefty pro controller for PS5. With a myriad of customisable features, including trigger travel length and even its weight, I’m going to break down whether this controller is worth your time.

The NACON Revolution 5 Unlimited is a big old pro controller, compatible with both PS5 and PC. It connects to PS5 via a dongle, can also connect wirelessly, offering 2.4Ghz connection for either, and offers Bluetooth connectivity too.

It features TMR thumbsticks, eradicating the worry of stick drift, along with swappable thumbstick tips and varying weights to fit in the grips of the controller, so you can customise the feel of the controller to your liking.

The big headliner here is a screen display in the centre of the controller, which allows access to simple customising menus without the need for an additional app — but we'll get into that later.

This Nacon Revolution 5 Unlimited will set you back £179.90/$229.90, actually making it one of the cheaper options in the pro controller market.

The NACON Revolution 5 Unlimited, which I’m just going to call the Rev5 from now on, comes in a rugged, hardshell case, with NACON branding embossed on the front.

Inside, the controller, of course, along with a collection of switchable thumbsticks, a D-Pad alternative, and weights which can be placed on the inside of the controller, a braided USB-A to C cable, the dongle, and the charging base.

The form factor is easily one of my favourite things about the Rev5. This is a pretty large, meaty controller, which, personally, I really like. It fills the hands, and immediately, all of the buttons feel like they are in naturally reachable places – something that wasn’t the case with the SCUF Omega, in my opinion.

Your eye will immediately be drawn to this little screen in the middle, and we’ll get to some of its features in a minute, but it definitely gives the Rev5 a premium look. The grips of the controller offer a ribbed rubber coating with a sleek black finish. The thumbsticks, d-pad, and triggers all have textured finishes, giving each a nice firm feel. There’s a satisfying clicky feel to the face buttons and back paddles, which are naturally placed where my fingers wrap around the back of the controller.

I love the triggers on this thing, which remind me of the Xbox controllers, actually. They have a nice smooth travel for the longer setting, but can also be switched to a mouse-like click, with a toggle on the back. I have to say, these are some of my favourite trigger length toggles that I’ve used on a pro controller. They are so easy to access and customise, without the need for longer nails to pick at them.

My only real complaints about the design are that the finish does make the controller a victim to smudges and smears, and the substitute button for the touchpad is a little small, which can be a pain if you want to quickly check leaderboards, for example.

Connecting this thing to the PS5 is a right doddle. You can use it wired with the braided cable, but most of my use was with the dongle.

What I really liked about this dongle is that it could be used whilst plugged into the back of the charging base, with a USB-A to C cable connecting to the PS5, meaning you can connect and charge the Rev5 with the use of just one USB-A port. However, if you're on the go, you can also just plug the dongle straight into the PS5, without the need for the charging base.

Annoyingly, however, you aren’t able to turn the PS5 on with this controller. You have to manually turn it on, then connect the Rev5, regardless of whether you are connecting wirelessly or wired.

Then there is that screen, which is really cool, but it did take me a moment to get my head around. A customise button on the top of the controller halts all inputs to the console and lets you navigate a simple menu system.

Here you can customise things like thumbstick dead zones, audio and mic input (if you’re using a wired headset), and customise each of the six additional buttons around the controller.

You’re then able to make four custom profiles, which you can switch between with a tap of the Profile button on the back of the controller. It’s not quite DualSense Edge levels of ease, but it is great.

If a little screen menu isn’t cutting it for you, there is also still the option to download the Nacon app and customise more intensely from there.

Then there is the physical customisation. You are able to switch out thumbsticks, the D-pad, and apply additional weights in the grips of the controllers. All of this is incredibly accessible, as there are no tools required. You can just pull one thing off and replace it with another. The only thing I had a bit of struggle getting off was the smaller variation of the d-pad.

Honestly, I think the Rev5 feels great. Once you have a profile that suits you, this thing is just moulded to the hand, with each of its additional paddles easily within reach, and its physical customisation options making it feel tailor-made to you.

I love the travel of the trigger if going for long triggers, but it features a really satisfying mouse-click if you customise it to short triggers too. The TMR sticks do have that weightless feel that's typical for thumbstick utilising Hall Effect tech, but I adjusted to it quite quickly.

The easy profile swapping and customisation on the actual controller, and the feel in the hand, meant I was more inclined than ever to just use this thing for regular games, not just those competitive titles like The Finals or Modern Warfare 4. I actually played most of Zero Parades using this controller, just because it was comfortable to use, despite not using a single customisation aspect.

There is a pretty big flaw, however, regarding that screen – the lack of a touchpad. The button initially used to replace it is very small and not as easy to touch as I’d like when opening up maps or menus in-game. Of course, you can just use one of the other shortcuts for this if you’re so inclined.

However, it does mean if there ever is a game that utilises the touchpad, like Ghost of Yotei, for example, you’re kind of out of luck. Admittedly, there isn’t a huge number of games that utilise this feature, or have anything beyond a single-use touch, so most of the time, it’s a bit of a non-issue. However, it is something to consider if this is to be your main controller.

As is the case with these controllers – and the same with the last Nacon controller I reviewed – this thing doesn’t feature rumble on the PS5, meaning it’s severely lacking in the immersive department.

For a lot of people, that’s just not going to matter, but for me it’s an additional feature that always brings me back to the DualSense Edge – a pro controller with full haptics and adaptive triggers. What’s even worse is that there is actually a rumble motor in this controller, but it’s limited to use on PC.

I can’t knock the controller too much for that because outside of the DualSense Edge, most pro controllers won't feature any form of rumble. It’s just a shame because, for me, if it had rumble on PS5, it would be among my favourite controllers.

Despite my musing over a lack of rumble support on PS5, I do think the Rev5 is worth considering if you’re in the market for a pro controller.

It feels fantastic in the hand, with a satisfying click and travel to each of its buttons; the customisation is easy to change from a software perspective, but also incredibly accessible from a hardware perspective.

It features great build quality, the charger/dongle system is handy, and it comes with a pretty cool carry case. And you get all of this for about £20 to £30 less than most other pro controllers.

Is it perfect? No way. But it’s a pretty damn nice controller.

#3992. Secretlab's ergonomics doctor told me this simple change would fix my neck pain, and they were right

This simple switch-up to my desk has made a massive difference

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

I've pretty much always carried an annoying, tense pain on the right side of my neck. And when I say always, I'm 29, and I remember going to see a physiotherapist about it when I was 18 - so you're talking my entire adult life. I tried everything: workouts, stretches, posture improvements, so you can probably imagine the mocking laugh that came out of me when, earlier this year, an ergonomics doctor at the Secretlab HQ told me all I needed was to switch my monitors around a bit.

But I should have had more faith in this sage, sage advice, because (alongside a renewed exercise routine to support it), the simple change to my setup actually did make a massive difference to my shoulder and neck pain. The only issue? The Secretlab products I needed to make it happen aren't the cheapest, but since they're now seeing discounts in the Black Friday Secretlab sale, I figure it's a good time to tell the story.

The TLDR here is that Secretlab's Vertical Monitor stand was all I needed to stop the constant strain of tension in my neck. If you want to skip the story and check it out on your own, it's available now in Secretlab's Black Friday or End-of-Year sale.

I met Dr. Lindsey “GamerDoc” Migliore at the Secretlab Singapore office back in April when I was invited to get a special early look at the then unannounced Secretlab Atlas. Myself and a few other UK journos were treated to an ergonomics session with Dr. Lindsey, a licensed physician and Esports medicine specialist who works with Esports athletes and organizations to optimize health and performance across both competitive and casual gaming.

Throughout the session, she made her way around the group, giving us a free clinic of sorts as we asked about our aches and pains and how we might improve our setups to remedy them. She roasted PCGamer's Jacob Ridley over his sitting position, but Secretlab's PR folks quickly pointed her at me because they knew I had an annoying pain in my neck.

Seeing as Dr. Lindsey applies principles of sports science, ergonomics, and performance medicine to gaming setups and actual Esports athletes, I was hoping for some technical, in-depth advice. Instead, she simply asked, "Do you have more than one monitor?"

"Yeah," I said, "I have one main one, and then a vertical one over on the right-hand side for Slack, Spotify, and other smaller apps when I'm working."

"And your pain is on which side?" she asked.

"You should try and put your secondary monitor up above your main one," Dr. Lindsey said with a smile. "That way, you won't be constantly craning your neck to the right and holding so much tension on that side".

I paused for a moment as I heard smirks emerging in the group. My eyebrows dropped, my eyes squinted. There's no way it's that simple, I thought to myself. Laughing it off, I retorted, "You sound crazy right now."

It was probably very disrespectful, but months later, after Secretlab called my bluff and supplied me with its various monitor arms to try, I feel like a total idiot.

Luckily, Dr. Lindsey took my feedback with great humour (even referring to me as a Celtic Jon Snow at one point), but for the record, I'd like to formally apologise for not taking her word as bond.

Turns out, stacking one monitor on top of the other made a world of difference, and despite the higher cost of Secretlab's vertical monitor stand, it's something I'd highly recommend to anyone who has more than one monitor on their gaming desk and struggles with similar pain to me. Lifting your head up to look at a monitor above your main eyeline is a much healthier repeated movement than constantly looking over to one direction - and no matter how good their head and neck support is, none of the best gaming chairs will change that.

I've now been using this monitor configuration for at least five or six months, and the difference in the neck pain I carry is massive. Thankfully, even though I don't own a Secretlab Magnus desk, I'm still able to make the brand's monitor arms work for me because they're compatible with other worktops so long as they meet the minimum thickness requirements for clamping them down securely.

Now, it should be said that alongside this monitor change, I've been doing a lot of exercise and gym work, which has no doubt done just as much to help things, so keep that in mind. I'm a firm believer that no one desk, monitor arm, or gaming chair is enough to cure your aches and pains without you putting in work alongside them.

Since originally taking on the vertical monitor stand and attaching both of my monitors to it, I've taken on a heavier OLED monitor as my main one, so I've also had to incorporate Secretlab's Heavy Duty Monitor Arm (also discounted in the Black Friday sale) to accommodate more than an 8kg load. It's a real shame you can't mix and match these. It'd be really cool if you could attach the stronger arm from the Heavy Duty variant to the vertical monitor stand, for example. Still, I can understand why the two aren't physically compatible.

The only other hesitation I have about Secretlab's vertical monitor stand is that it's expensive. For context, there are plenty listed at Amazon, like Standopia's and AVLT's which come in at $79.99 at Amazon and $99.99 at Amazon respectively.

Yes, with Secretlab's, you can attach all sorts to it if you wish. With room for four Doc Ock-like limbs extending out from it, you could have four monitors like a stock broker, two monitors and a tablet or music stand of some description, maybe a camera, or whatever you can make work. But even grabbing it with just two arms, it's a very pricey desk attachment. That's why I've chosen my moment to recommend it to you a little cheaper during Secretlab's Black Friday sale. If your budget can stretch to this monitor configuration with its small discount, I'd recommend it. Especially with Secretlab's build quality giving you peace of mind. If not, there are loads of cheaper alternatives linked below.

#3991. Review: GTA 6 (Xbox) - The Most Breathtaking Open-World Game Of All Time

This is going to dominate your life for months!

Where do you even start with a game like GTA 6? Not only is it the most highly-anticipated video game we've ever seen, but it's also attempting to live up to ridiculous expectations set by its predecessors over the years. GTA 3 revolutionised how we thought about 3D open-world epics, Vice City and San Andreas pushed things to the next level, GTA 4 took yet another massive step into the HD era, and GTA 5 propelled the series into another stratosphere.

We've all spent the last 13 years trying to figure out what GTA 6 might look like by the time it arrives, and the answer is perhaps more simplistic than some had theorised - it's basically GTA 5 mixed with Red Dead Redemption 2, but with a ton of added detail and ambition on top. That's all it needed to be, and I reckon people are going to absolutely love it.

Before we get to the open world, which is surely the most incredible aspect of the entire game, we should first touch on the story of Lucia and Jason. These two amateur criminals accidentally run into each other and establish a relationship (which can alter between platonic and romantic depending on how you interact throughout the campaign), and after a simple score goes wrong, they find themselves being dragged into more and more dangerous scenarios. That's the basic premise, and the rest is up for you to discover yourself.

The GTA 6 Extended Preview from a few months ago left me very concerned about whether there was enough intrigue to the two main characters (along with the NPCs for that matter), but I needn't have worried. Lucia is a fiesty, hot-headed personality - the type of person who thinks less about the consequences and more about the high life she's determined to acquire - while Jason is extremely laid back to a hilarious extent at times, although also highly capable in pretty much any situation he finds himself in. The two bounce off each other really nicely, and their dynamic definitely remains engaging throughout the campaign's duration.

While I really don't want to spoil anything story-related, the mission structure is very much what you'd expect from GTA 5 and RDR2. In other words, there's a well-balanced mix of laid-back and humorous missions along with more intense shootouts and getaways that significantly ramp up in intensity. They've managed to get really inventive and ambitious with some of the later missions in particular, and I think there's no doubt they're the best of any GTA game.

I also want to point out the use of music in GTA 6's missions, which caught me off-guard and became one of my low-key favourite features. In a nutshell, if you find yourself in the likes of a shootout or a getaway, you'll often notice that curated tunes play in the background to amplify the situation. The developers sometimes even go a step further by making the lighting around you pulsate to the beat, or by introducing lyricists to create a menacing vibe, and it can turn an otherwise generic mission into an amazing one. Seriously, I can't overstate how much I love this feature.

The story itself takes 40ish hours if you completely rush it (which admittedly I've been doing for the most part to hit this embargo), but if you take your time and do at least a decent amount of the optional stuff, it's likely more around 60-100+ hours. As I say, I've enjoyed all of those hours, and I think the campaign seriously hits its stride in the final third - the vast majority of memorable moments are saved for the latter stages.

I don't want you to fixate on the 40-100+ hour figure though, and that's because GTA 6's open world is so incredible and so vast that you could be playing it for months, and likely years, and not see everything it has to offer. We've never seen a GTA world like this - traffic levels are extremely high, the number of NPCs on the streets is ridiculous, it always feels like something's happening around every corner (there are so many random encounters!), you'll find loads of buildings you can go into, there's so much detail on everything... it's just an absolute dream for anyone who loves the idea of immersing themselves in this game.

GTA 5 had an amazing open world too, but after going back and playing it for the purpose of this review, there are two major differences that stand out - there's far less actually happening in the world at any one time (and therefore much less to interact with), and the map just feels tiny in comparison. GTA 6's state of Leonida incorporates so much more than just Vice City itself, including many other highly-populated areas such as Key Lento and Ambrosia. The first time you actually see Vice City in a mission (assuming you haven't gone and explored it previously) is a highlight of the entire game - it immediately appears so vast and so incredibly detailed that it feels like a next-gen experience.

The way in which you interact with that world as a player has evolved as well. Cops are smarter than ever, and not only prove a tough challenge when attempting a getaway at three stars or more, but they also remember what you look like - and therefore you sometimes have to disguise yourself by changing into different outfits. Stealing a car now requires you to think about what kind of lock system it has on it, and whether there's a tracker fitted that will alert the police to your location. Cars can even run out of fuel now! Every element feels more in-depth than we've seen in GTA in the past, but Rockstar has crucially balanced the impact just right, so it's never to the detriment of your ability to just have fun.

I do think you'll get the most out of the game if you pace yourself though. It feels intentionally designed to encourage a slow playstyle where you explore, hang out, browse the fully-featured social media and news feeds on your phone (complete with video clips and comment sections), take part in games like pool and minigolf, engage in countless side-missions and random encounters, watch and play a ridiculous amount of purpose-built content on your in-game TV, and ultimately just see what you can discover without rapidly jumping from mission-to-mission. The amount of content here is overwhelming, but in a really satisfying way.

Of course, it's almost a given at this point that GTA 6 looks visually incredible, and I can confirm that it's definitely a stunner on Xbox Series X. There's some occasional pop-in, but it's minimal, and I only ran into a few tiny bugs during the review period (which may have been ironed out for release anyway). The performance is mostly very smooth considering the circumstances as well - yes, it's a bit jarring at first to go back to 30FPS if you've been playing 60FPS games for the most part in recent years, but give it an hour-or-two, and you probably won't care anymore. Seriously, it's a total non-issue for me at this point, and I'm more than happy playing at 30FPS.

It should be noted that I played around 30 hours on a VRR-enabled display during the review period, and around 10 hours without one. I was perfectly happy with the performance in both cases, with the only noticeably big frame rate drops occurring during very rare and visually intensive gameplay sequences.

So, is there anything I don't like about GTA 6? The only thing I'd say is that it doesn't top my tier list in terms of greatest GTA stories ever, although it's probably still in the top three. It's a narrative that'll fully invest most players from start to finish, and there are shocking moments and twists that are bound to last long in the memory, but I also reckon it gets a bit too convoluted and farcical at times. That said, the final third of the campaign is jam-packed with intense story elements and incredibly action-packed missions, guaranteeing some truly jaw-dropping moments.

Its tone can also feel overly harsh and uncomfortably serious in specific circumstances, but hey... this is Grand Theft Auto after all. Every GTA has its moments like that, but the impact feels more striking this time due to the enhanced sense of realism. Fortunately, there's plenty of lighthearted humour to be found along the way as well.

Somehow, GTA 6 lives up to the hype. Rockstar Games has crafted the most incredible open world I've ever experienced in a video game, packed with so much detail that I'll want to continue exploring it for months and likely years to come. It's coupled with a campaign that's full of extremely entertaining missions, led by two main characters who I've become much more invested in than I'd anticipated.

I'd have been fuming if you'd told me in 2013 that I'd have to wait 13 more years for the next GTA game, but now that it's finally here, I'm just relieved they've somehow managed to pull off another Game of the Decade contender once again.

I don't know what Edwin's been feeding the Maw in my off week, but when I entered its chambers this morning it had left game releases everywhere. Ceiling, walls, floor, they all glisten with games of every size and genre. Even after I hosed away the ones largely made with the assistance of generative AI, the sifting sieves fitted across the drains held a bounty of interesting releases.

Let's get to it, then, before the Maw wakes up and realises I've nabbed all its spoils.

Well, that was potentially too many games in all, even after striking out a fair few that were on my list when I started writing this round up.

It's a busy week for us in the warehouse. Edwin's putting the finishing touches on a series of features he's been working on for months, I'm getting the RPS 100 ready to go live next week, James is wrangling the advent calendar, Mark is working on a write up of a tasty expansion pack, and the guides team are getting everything in order head of the release of GTA 6 next week. #3988. GTA 6 release day live coverage – all the latest news and updates

Join the GamesRadar community for quick access. Enter your email below and we'll send confirmation, and sign you up to our newsletter.

Keep exploring and earning more as a member.

Get the biggest gaming news, reviews, and releases straight to your inbox.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

It's weird to type this out, but the GTA 6 release is finally upon us after a 13-year wait.

Red Dead Redemption 2 launched to acclaim at the time to ease the wait, though few things in gaming feel as big an event as a Grand Theft Auto release from Rockstar.

And thankfully, the wait looks to be worth it. The GamesRadar+ GTA 6 review lands on a perfect score, and says "Rockstar hasn't just set a new benchmark, it has delivered the highest-fidelity sandbox of the generation." It's not just us, either. The GTA 6 Metacritic score is a good 'un. In fact, only the OG Zelda: Ocarina of Time can match it.

So, we're probably on the same page. It's time to get the download going, and thoughts to our gaming brethren on PC who don't own a console.

To celebrate the moment, we're firing up the live blog to put everything you need to know in one, evolving space – from review buzz to launch requirements to exactly how the GTA 6 release time rollout is working. On that note, let's crack on.

And here we go! It may be GTA 6 release time for some sooner than others, but we'll all end up there eventually, right? So let's get into some things you'll need to know.

First things first. The main talking point today, as we count down the hours to launch, is critics' verdicts on GTA 6. As per our own GTA 6 review, we've landed on a perfect score.

"GTA 6 is the highest-fidelity sandbox of its generation," he says. "Rockstar has built an open world of truly astonishing scale, scope, and quality. There's a degree of sophistication to everything GTA 6 does, and there's no aspect of the series' gameplay that hasn't been improved over past installments."

We're not the only ones who dig this one either. The GTA 6 Metacritic score ranks it among the most popular games of all time. The only competition is The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time. The original one, that is. Mind you, the remake is pretty nifty, too.

So! The game is good, though I have an inkling that plenty of you have already pre-ordered it. According to Sensor Tower, Rockstar has already made $1.45 billion from GTA 6, aided by nearly 90% of us buying the controversial $100 Ultimate Edition. Oof!

I imagine a few more people will be tossing some more money Rockstar's way.

So, for many of you who are jumping in, some housekeeping. First, the GTA 6 release time.

Rockstar isn't setting a singular time for people to jump in, so some of you will be playing sooner than others. Namely, congratulations to those of you who live in New Zealand or who know the trick. If you don't, our guide on how to play GTA 6 early with the New Zealand trick will sort you out.

If you've got some hours to wait, you're not alone. That said, you can still be productive. There's a new PS5 update you'll need to download to play GTA 6.

Sony hasn't confirmed what's behind the update, though we've got a good guess. Amid an AI explosion, PS5 jailbreaks have become more frequent in the run-up to GTA 6. Not only does that risk the latest Grand Theft Auto game being released before its official release date, but it could also result in it unofficially ending up on PC. Not ideal, no.

As we near release, though, it looks like Sony has managed ot hold this one off.

If you weren't already convinced, the GTA 6 reviews put Rockstar's latest in a good position for the upcoming Game Awards. Just yesterday, we found out that GTA 6 is up for several awards, including Game of the Year.

While that has led a few people to ask how that can be the case when it's not out yet, host Geoff Keighley has chimed in to add that reviewers behind the nominations have been playing it for three weeks. So, there is some reasoning to the inclusion.

You know it's a big day when none other than Rockstar president Sam Houser issues a rare statement. Here it is in full:

"Rockstar Games was founded on the belief that games could achieve the same distinction as all other forms of storytelling, become essential to modern culture, and to be thought of as stories and worlds that live on with all of us.

"This week, Grand Theft Auto returns to Leonida and modern-day Vice City. While things have changed and time has passed, one aspect holds true: We have tried to create an experience that will exceed your expectations while showing what this medium is capable of, and why we believe games are so special. Whether you can trace your journey to this game through the entire series or are experiencing Grand Theft Auto for the first time, this is a narrative set in a world full of possibilities — and it is up to you as the player to shape how it ultimately feels, and concludes. We hope it felt both familiar and entirely new, and above all, we hope that you had fun.

"We are incredibly grateful to you and everything that you do to celebrate games. We look forward to many more years of sharing these experiences with you."

As we wind down the live blog for the day, here's a fun one for you. One of the many mad details of GTA 6 is that all of its refrigerators sound different. It's all in the details, baby.

"Much of the dynamic soundscape is informed by the incredibly detailed art throughout the world," says audio VP Alastair MacGregor.

"One small example is that convenience store refrigerators all have their own unique sounds. In a run-down store, the refrigerators and freezers are loud and sound like they are badly maintained. Their compressor units can be heard mechanically whirring away from years of neglect.

"As a result, the bottles behind the doors can be heard shaking and the units click on and off more frequently. In an up-market store, the refrigerators are quieter, adding a subtle hum to the environment."

Game of the year, people. Game of the year.

#3987. "The lesson learned is you can have both": Skyrim lead designer reckons there's merit in Baldur's Gate 3-style tough choices and Bethesda's do-anything approach

How many doors should be open at any point in an adventure?

Whether RPGs are better off prioritising player freedom or endeavouring to have several doors slam shut every time you put another foot forwards in order to encourage multiple runs with different characters is, to put it bluntly, something I reckon will still be a matter of debate in the year 4000. We'll all have evolved in non-corporeal beings floating in a galaxy that's been racked by such change that even the six million copies of The Elder Scrolls 5 we've littered the Earth with will have been swept away into the great recycling bin on the gods' desktop, and there'll still be sniping going on about whether it's ok that Skyrim lets you be a master thiefssassin who leads the companions, knows every spell under the sun, and slapped up a world-eating dragon for fun.

For what it's worth, the game's lead designer reckons both games that do and don't let you do that have their merits when executed well.

Speaking to The Examined Game, ex-Bethesda dev Bruce Nesmith talked about being "pleasantly surprised" when playing Baldur's Gate 3 just how much he enjoyed making "consequential decisions that closed off gameplay". In Nesmith's view, Larian "redefined things in a certain way" with their take on the D&D universe and the fantasy rules it plays by. However, he argued that there's still merit to taking an approach more akin to Bethesda's post-Morrowind Elder Scrolls entries and striving to make it possible for the player to see the majority of what the game has to offer in a single playthrough.

"They were both fun," he said. "They were just fun in different ways and that to me was part of the surprise. I would have expected to fall on one side or the other, as if they were things that you couldn't have both [of]. The lesson learned is you can have both. I can enjoy this game over here that does it this way and enjoy this game over here that does it that way."

Nesmith made clear that he still thinks the idea of, with a few exceptions like Skyrim's civil war, not gating the player off from the likes of doing multiple faction questlines is a "very good philosophy" that he supports.

As much as it's always a bit of a cop out to declare that everything's equally good, actually, I do think that there's merit in both approaches. I love the dedication the likes of New Vegas, Disco Elysium, and The Witcher 2 have to making you pick a path and see where it takes you at the expense of not seeing other stuff. Hell, the latter game's infamous for being totally different depending on who you choose to waltz off with at the end of the opening act.

That said, Skyrim's open-endedness was undoubtedly one of the factors which made it so easy for me to get majorly into when I was just cutting my teeth in RPGs as a teenager. There's value in such games existing, even if for plenty it might be as a gateway drug to games with crunchier and more challenging narratives that do demand you plug in your brain and carefully consider every choice you make. Whether there's still as much value in being the gateway drug nowadays compared to in 2011 is the question The Elder Scrolls 6'll likely answer whenever it rocks up. Coming as it is after the likes of BG3 and The Witcher 3 have had near Skyrim-level gangbusters success while leaning a lot more heavily into the hard stuff typically pegged as having less potential for mass appeal.

For what it's worth, while you can very much argue about the execution, Fallout 4's main quest was a lot more choice-heavy than Fallout 3's. So, Bethesda may well opt to pivot or make compromises in their player freedom-first ways if they feel some crunchier choice is in order.

#3986. UK's Health Service Issues Warning Over GTA 6, Urges Players to Take Care of Their Hands

GTA 6 is so massive that even the UK's National Health Service — commonly known as the NHS — has gotten in on the act.

To be fair, the NHS raises a good point with regards to the open world game's imminent release. On Instagram, it's urging players to take regular breaks in order to avoid issues like repetitive strain injury — or RSI for short.

In a cruel twist, the official account's admin has actually had to undergo surgery to fix their problem, meaning that playing GTA 6 at launch is going to be difficult.

"Thoughts and prayers for your admin. Bit of surgery to remove a lump. Great NHS service, bad timing," the post reads.

"Planning on dedicating time to gaming later this week? Try and take regular breaks, obviously. And be mindful of RSI," it continues.

In this case, RSI is caused by overuse of certain muscles in the hands and fingers, brought about by repeated actions. It's a pretty common injury amongst gamers, and without wanting to scare you off completely, it can lead to lasting damage if you refuse to properly rest the impacted area.

The NHS has got a whole page on RSI if you want more information.

Have you ever had an RSI? Remember to pause your game in the comments section below.

#3985. Capcom Officially Reveals Sixth Mega Man: Dual Override Robot Master

"This nautical nemesis unleashes a typhoon of tyranny"

Capcom is bringing Mega Man: Dual Override to the Switch 1 & 2 in 2027 and to build some excitement, it's been revealing the Robot Masters you'll be facing in the game.

This week it's officially announced the sixth Robot Master, 'Boat Man'. Here's the official description, along with a look (via Rockman Corner):

A coastal fishing robot with a timid nature, Boat Man drops anchor in Mega Man: Dual Override! Teased for being hesitant to venture the high seas, this nautical nemesis unleashes a typhoon of tyranny against all who doubt him!

As our sixth Robot Master, Boat Man casts a wide net against those that ridiculed him. Will he bait you into his tidal trap? Or will you take the plunge into his aquatic arena to battle him willingly?"

This follows Capcom announcing the winner of the Mega Man: Dual Override Robot Master design contest earlier this week. It's "Cleanser Man"!

These Robot Masters will be joined by Cook Man, Tank Man, Twinkle Girl and Jet Man, with more Robot Master Reveals to come.

#3984. Roundup: Here's What The Critics Are Saying About GTA 6 So Far

Are we looking at the highest-rated game of 2026?

The first reviews for GTA 6 are officially out now, and as you've probably already seen, we've got one here at Pure Xbox! We gave the game an "Outstanding" 10/10, which isn't entirely surprising considering the history of this series.

But what about everyone else? GTA 6 is nominated for Game of the Year at The Game Awards, so does it live up to that recommendation? Are the critics overwhelmingly enamoured with it? That's what we've been intrigued to find out.

So, here's what the critics are saying about GTA 6 so far:

"Somehow, GTA 6 lives up to the hype. Rockstar Games has crafted the most incredible open world I've ever experienced in a video game, packed with so much detail that I'll want to continue exploring it for months and likely years to come."

Review GTA 6 (Xbox) - The Most Breathtaking Open-World Game Of All Time

This is going to dominate your life for months!

"GTA 6 is the deepest, densest, most accomplished open world since Red Dead Redemption 2. Rockstar has set a new sandbox standard here, with a world that feels alive and populated with real people; Leonida is a place where it appears almost anything can happen at any time."

Review GTA 6 (PS5) - The Greatest Open World Game Ever Made

"A game so good I asked our tech team if I could somehow give it 11/10. GTA 6 is an absolute masterclass in genre-mashing. With meticulous detailing and levels of immersion that almost feel dangerous, it's steeped in steamy satire — with story beats that often cut close to home as they relish in laugh-out-loud absurdity. Given the state of the industry, it's sobering that we might never see another game like this again. Grand Theft Auto 6 is a cover-to-cover masterpiece without equal."

"Grand Theft Auto VI is a generational game that stands toe-to-toe with many of the great crime stories and satires across other media. It showcases both the entertainment value of interactive play and the current high-water mark for technical and artistic detail in games. Hunt for and count up all the minor faults or foibles you like, but then note how you just spent another hour lost in this remarkable escape into criminality, wanton violence, egregious sex, and the elusive potential of true love."

"This game is the culmination of everything the developer has previously achieved in the open-world space that pushes the genre to heights that, in all likelihood, no other developer will be able to reach. GTA 6 is an astonishing open-world action game that I’d wager won’t be outdone until Grand Theft Auto 7."

"GTA 6 is the highest-fidelity sandbox of its generation. Rockstar has built an open world of truly astonishing scale, scope, and quality. There's a degree of sophistication to everything GTA 6 does, and there's no aspect of the series' gameplay that hasn't been improved over past instalments."

"I regularly find myself in love with video games, but it’s extraordinarily rare that I find myself in complete awe of them. Put simply, Grand Theft Auto 6 is the single most impressive video game I have ever played."

"A game of opposites and awe, minute detail and impossible scale, Rockstar pushes back the horizon of video games once again with GTA 6. An irreducible mix of silliness, intimacy, grand ideas and rock 'n' roll action - and a load more after that."

"Grand Theft Auto VI delivers a remarkably immersive and ambitious open-world experience, blending thrilling gameplay, diverse activities, and a compelling relationship between Jason and Lucia. While uneven storytelling, pacing issues, and occasional performance drops prevent it from reaching perfection, the richly realized world of Leonida and its extraordinary attention to detail make this an unforgettable crime adventure that largely lives up to its monumental expectations."

"Grand Theft Auto VI is a great game that lives up to so much of the hype and expectations. Lucia and Jason are a well-written and compelling pair of protagonists, and the side characters you meet on their journey are great, even if the need to constantly raise the stakes across such a long story lessens its impact. You do have so much more freedom with how to tackle missions, though, and Leonida is a world filled with things to do and discover that will keep you coming back for a long time."

As you can see, GTA 6 is a darling of the critics right now, and its initial rating on Metacritic sits at a whopping 99, which makes it the highest-rated game of 2026 (and literally the joint best game of all time if it keeps up this pace).

It should be noted that the vast majority of reviews are for the PS5 version, but both the PlayStation and Xbox versions are both sitting at 99 as things stand. That figure will probably change, but not to any significant degree.

History tells us that we should have always expected a mainline Grand Theft Auto game to get incredible review scores, but it was really hard to see how they'd live up to expectations with this one. Nevertheless, they've somehow done it!

#3983. Microsoft workers accuse company of trying to get customers "addicted" to AI while forcing it on their own staff and making them party to "human rights violations"

Open letter warns of "a cascade of business and ethics risks"

A group of "concerned Microsoft workers" have published an open letter criticising their employer's "speed-at-all-costs" approach to generative AI, which they argue is "harming our customers, colleagues, shareholders, vendors, and the planet". They accuse Microsoft leadership of trying to get people "addicted" to genAI, while making their own staff miserable by mandating AI usage.

Echoing the on-going BDS campaign against Microsoft's Xbox business, the writers contend that Microsoft have become party to "human rights violations" by selling generative AI technology to Israel's military during the latter's invasion of Gaza, which a UN commission has deemed a genocide. They're also critical of Microsoft's contracts with the USA's draconian Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency. While seemingly not against generative AI in principle, they're organising against "the AI industry’s trajectory to continue to enrich AI’s powerful few", pointing out that AI companies now account for a terrifying share of the global stock market.

I know about the letter thanks to Vertical Slice, who cite a New York Times report on Microsoft's recent voluntary buyouts, which follow several waves of mass layoffs at a company with a market value of around $4 trillion.

"For many, working at Microsoft has become joyless and demoralizing, with job satisfaction declining around the same time the company accelerated its AI investments," the workers write. "Crushing workloads, threats of AI job replacement and layoffs, constantly shifting business priorities, and re-orgs destabilize our work environment and erode employee trust in leadership."

The letter organisers complain that "workers are forced to use AI in almost every work area, with little to no training and no strategic rationale besides 'speed'," obliging them to spend a lot of time "learning and relearning tools, fixing AI slop, and reworking or rolling back low-quality features". They feel that Microsoft's generative AI strategy is exposing customers "to overreliance, misuse, and physical and mental harm", not least because "our own research shows that AI agents don’t prioritize user safety, and internal planning documents detail how to 'make people addicted' to AI products." If that last part is an actual quote from an internal feature document, then: yeeeeeeesh.

The writers further take issue with Microsoft's investments in data centers for generative AI use, which may use up a lot of water while contributing to carbon emissions (jeopardising Microsoft's older commitments to reducing their carbon footprint). They note that "our Community-First AI Infrastructure plan makes vague financial and job-creation commitments, but doesn’t address greenhouse gas emissions or other damage already being done."

The organisers also call out their employer for becoming "a partner to human rights violations" by licensing generative AI tools to the Israeli military and ICE. "Not only are we risking reputational, financial, and legal damage, we are allowing our AI products to be used against whole communities for mass surveillance, detainment, deportation, and genocide," they write.

Finally, they take a swing at "Microsoft’s participation in circular investment across a handful of AI leaders " - that is, AI companies pouring cash into each other, which naturally creates the risk of several companies biting the dust if one company's fortunes take a tumble. This ouroboros strategy "exposes workers, customers, shareholders, and society to a cascade of business and ethics risks," the writers claim, noting that AI-linked stocks now dominate the S&P 500 index.

The letter writers have a number of demands. They'd like more say over "AI product strategy decisions", and for Microsoft to consider customer feedback and bring different development disciplines together "to help guard against shipping AI-worsened user experiences". They want Microsoft to "offer quality training and empower workers to integrate AI in their workflows without tying AI use to rewards, reprimand or layoffs." They call on the execs to "end unfair AI-driven workforce reductions and agree to worker protections".

Looking beyond Microsoft's walls, the workers argue that "job opportunities from data center investments are mostly temporary" and that "Microsoft must protect all workers, not attempt to avoid the unionized trades in local communities, and ensure a just transition for all impacted workers."

The letter writers call on Microsoft to "expand Responsible AI and Sensitive Use teams and fund programs to communicate potential harms to users". They would like Microsoft to stop selling AI materials to organisations "if they are engaged in violence, mass surveillance, detainment, deportation, or genocide", requesting that Microsoft "transparently share contracts with all governments and their agencies or contractors, including police and armed forces, and immediately terminate any contracts with those directly or indirectly involved in human rights violations."

The letter writers want Microsoft to "reduce financial dependency on OpenAI and other AI partners and provide transparency into all AI investments". In general, they want their bosses to "stop offloading financial risk to workers, vendors, partners, customers, and shareholders through irresponsible investments and relationships." As regards the environment, the workers are demanding that Microsoft "reaffirm our goal to be carbon negative, water positive, and zero waste by 2030". They want Microsoft to cooperate more with environmental regulators, and "to respect local communities by rejecting dirty energy, engaging fairly and transparently, and refusing to build in resource-scarce areas."

It's not clear who, exactly, is behind the letter, or how many others at Microsoft have signed as of writing. I've requested comment from Microsoft, and will update this piece as and when I hear more.

Your Criminal Profile in Grand Theft Auto 6 is your reputation, similar to an honor or morality system

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Actions have consequences in Grand Theft Auto 6. Building on the honor system in Red Dead Redemption 2, fully functional Criminal Profiles in GTA 6 not only keep track of the way that you're playing the game, but help dictate how the world (and the characters who inhabit it) react to Jason and Lucia's presence.

GTA 6 Criminal Profiles are a really important metric that can change fundamental aspects of your play experience. I'm going to help you understand all of this with an overview of the Criminal Profiles in GTA 6, and offer up some tips on how you can change through the five tiers.

Your actions and behavior are captured in real-time by the Criminal Profile system. You are able to quickly check the status of your current criminal profile for both Jason and Lucia by holding right on the d-pad – look for the little icons next to their profile pictures for an update at a glance.

For a deeper dive navigate to the "Jason & Lucia" menu. These profiles change over time, and their status can have a lasting impact on each of the characters so you will want to check this frequently.

Jason and Lucia each have their own individual Criminal Profiles, but the actions of one character can influence the behavior of the other when you're out on the streets together.

There are five Criminal Profiles in GTA 6 that Lucia and Jason can move between, all of which are laid out below from least to most severe.

It's possible to move freely between Professional, Hardened, Violent, and Psycho tiers. However, should you create enough chaos to be considered Irredeemable this is an irreversible trait – and one which may permanently impact your relationship status in GTA 6.

Weekly digests, tales from the communities you love, and more

Professional and Hardened Criminal Profiles are assigned to characters who do their best to avoid violence, and at least attempt to resolve situations without incident. Start pursuing extreme violence and cruelty to both animals and civilians and you'll become to etch into Violent and Psycho territories.

While you're on a mission, Criminal Profiles aren't affected by any criminal acts that the game requires you to do. It's only when you go beyond what is truly necessary or reasonable that action begins to have consequences in either direction.

Below your health bar is where the GTA 6 flashes up little icons which denote how your actions are impacting your criminal profile. The game will track low-casualty incursions and clean getaways, just as it will acts of extreme violence and destruction.

If your character is going in a direction you aren't happy with, here's what to be aware of with each Criminal Profile:

If you're after a Criminal Profile that lists you as a 'Professional' then you'll need to be considerate of your actions. Avoid casualties where possible, don't chase unnecessary aggression, and only do what could be considered reasonable to get the task at hand completed.

It's worth noting that making threats won't impact your Professional Criminal Profile, and that the best way to maintain this reputation is to avoid violence unless you're threatened and to try to remain undetected while committing crimes. This isn't always possible, just don't escalate for the sake of it.

Tip: Non-lethal incapacitations (aiming for joints rather than the head or heart), thoughtful actions, and petting every dog and cat you come across will increase your Focus in GTA 6 while you have a Professional Criminal Profile.

If you've found yourself with a Hardened Criminal Profile in GTA 6, it probably means that you've started to resort to violence to complete your objectives. Rushing to kill enemies and breaking detection for the sake of it will contribute to this profile – although it's still easy enough to get back to a Professional Criminal Profile if you take steps to avoid violence in a couple of robberies.

If you continue down this path, harming civilians and killing cops, then your Criminal Profile will eventually shift from Hardened to Violent. It's worth flagging that, like the Professional profile, non-lethal incapacitations will still contribute to an increase in your focus.

If you've gotten yourself a Violent Criminal Profile in GTA 6 then something has gone really wrong. This is the game reflecting that you've probably spent a fair few hours attacking cops and civilians for the smallest infractions. Brutally attacking cops and shooting fleeing civilians in the back will contribute to your Violent profile but acting in a self-defensive capacity will not.

If you find yourself pushing into Psycho territory, it is still possible to move back to Hardened or Professional. You'll just need to be more conscious about the way you are interacting with the world, and become more deliberate with your actions.

Tip: Headshots will increase your focus if you've gotten yourself a Violent profile, but each one of those will also make it more difficult to return to Hardened or Professional state.

You know what you're doing, and you don't care who knows about it. If you get assigned the Psycho Criminal Profile in GTA 6 then you've most likely spent a few hours mercilessly harming vulnerable animals (yes, hunting does count in certain instances), murdering defenseless civilians with abandon, and have been blasting through cops with no hesitation.

Something to note with the Psycho profile is that there is an additional icon you should keep an eye out for. If you see a line-scratch through the icon, it means you've reached a breaking point and are at risk of tipping into Irredeemable territory. Start shooting to incapacitate to get back to being a reasonable member of society.

If you continue acting with wild abandon once you reach the breaking point within the Psycho boundaries, eventually you will earn yourself an Irredeemable Criminal Profile in GTA 6. This is only given to the worst of the worst – this would have been Trevor's starting point in GTA 5 – and reflects your insistence on creating maximum chaos, regardless of the cost.

This level of excessive violence will make you irredeemable, which is permanently attributed to your character. This will impact the way civilians react to you on the street, it will drive a wedge between Jason and Lucia, and will change the way cops approach you too. If you've got a Psycho or Irredeemable Criminal Profile, expect cops to start open firing at you far faster than before.

Having a Psycho or Irredeemable profile will mean that headshots increase your focus, which is a great way to engage in gunplay. However, you'll also lose the ability to surrender to the cops – which can have a pretty big impact on your money in GTA 6.

#3981. Cyberattack on Sega third-party newsletter distributor reportedly sees over two million email addresses leaked, but Sega accounts unaffected

Japanese email distribution firm Arara were the target of the attack

Sega have revealed that over two million email addresses have leaked due to a cyberattack on Japanese email delivery provider Arara, whom the Like A Dragon and Sonic publishers use to distribute newsletters. Sega and Arara are currently busy investigating what happened in the breach, which doesn't appear to have affected the Sega accounts you can use receive in-game rewards and access a calendar which reminds you when it's Kazuma Kiryu's birthday. The companies have urged those who signed up for the affected newsletters to be wary of potential phishing attempts.

According to Automaton, who've translated Sega's official press release about the cyberattack, 2,196,044 email addresses in total were affected. 92,273 of that number were linked to the newsletter distribution.

The company have listed some specific newsletter releases as having been affected, including two exhibition announcements for this year's Tokyo Game Show, the announcement of arcade rhythm game Chunithm Mate's launch, six newsletters about online character lottery service Sega Lucky Kuji Online, the launch of a rhythm game update dubbed Ongeki Re:Fresh Act.2, and the launch of another arcade rhythm game update called Maimai DX MAGiCAL. Number one, that's a lot of rhythm games, and number two, Sega have advised those who opted in and received those newsletters to watch out for fishing emails from people posing as being tied to Sega or Arara.

Sega reportedly confirmed that - as far as the affected emails go - no names, dates of birth, genders, residential addresses, phone numbers, credit card information, and passwords are known to have been leaked. There had also been no reports of cases where the leaked information had been misused as of the time Sega made their announcement. The company have naturally put distributing any further email newsletters through Arara on hold until their investigation's done and plan to reach out to each affected person individually once the full details of the leak have been confirmed.

While data breaches and cyberattacks are nothing new, there have been a fair few recently, with both Street Fighter makers Capcom and Kingdom Come Deliverance 2 devs Warhorse suffering incidents of their own last month.

#3980. PlayStation Has No GOTY Nominee at The Game Awards for First Time in 12 Years

For the first time in 12 years — since all the way back in 2014 — there is no Sony-published PlayStation title amongst The Game Awards' Game of the Year nominees.

In that time, Sony has won three Game of the Year awards at Geoff's annual show, making it the most successful publisher in the event's history.

But its over-a-decade streak of nominations will finally come to an end here in 2026, as none of its releases from this year have made the cut.

That includes God of War: Sons of Sparta, Marathon, MLB The Show 26, Saros, Marvel Tokon: Fighting Souls, and Marvel's Wolverine.

In particular, Saros and Marvel Tokon got really strong reviews, but given just how stacked this year's competition is, it's no real surprise to see these relatively niche titles be left in the cold.

At the start of the year, many would have probably predicted that Wolverine would be in the mix — but a lukewarm critical reception has ultimately sealed its fate.

Just to recap, this year's Game of the Year nominees are as follows:

Again, since 2015, there hasn't been a single year where a Sony-published title has been ignored. Here's a full list of Sony's nominees in that time:

I don't think anyone would deny that Sony and its PlayStation Studios have had an off year. While their output has actually been quite frequent, none of their latest releases have made a lasting impact in the way that many of the above titles did in their respective years.

Do you think any of Sony's 2026 PS5 games deserved to be nominated for Game of the Year? Claw something out in the comments section below.
